Under the 1909 Act the synchronized sound recording shared the film's single copyright; because that copyright was not renewed (see print layer), the original synchronized track is also in the public domain. editorial:
"Any Old Port!" is a 21-minute pre-Code sound comedy short produced by Hal Roach Studios and released by MGM on March 5, 1932â€”note the queue records it as 1930, but that year does not match the theatrical release date. Directed by James W. Horne from an original script by H.M. Walker, it casts Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy as merchant sailors who stumble into a seedy hotel run by the villainous Mugsie Long (Walter Long), who is forcing a young woman (Jacqueline Wells, later known as Julie Bishop) into marriage. The film builds to an extended boxing-ring finale: Oliver manages from ringside while Stanâ€”unaware he is facing the local championâ€”is put into the ring. The synchronized score was composed by Marvin Hatley and Leroy Shield, the Hal Roach house composers responsible for the signature musical texture of the entire L&H sound era.

Hal Roach Studios did not renew the copyright. Under the 1909 Copyright Act, renewal was mandatory in the 28th year of the termâ€”1959 for a film published in 1932, or 1957â€“58 if the original registration was somehow dated 1930. Searches of both the 1958 and the 1959 Catalog of Copyright Entries (Parts 12â€“13, Motion Pictures, Third Series) show no renewal entry for this title, confirming the copyright lapsed. The print and the original synchronized audio track are accordingly in the public domain. The live rights trap is trademark: the Laurel & Hardy names, likenesses, and the derby-and-cravat persona are actively managed by successor licensing entities, and building a commercial productâ€”packaging, merchandise, brandingâ€”around those characters requires separate trademark clearance even though the film footage itself is free to use.
faq: Is the film footage free to download, cut, and redistribute?

Yes. Hal Roach Studios failed to renew the copyright in 1959, so the print is in the public domain. You can download, edit, and distribute the footage. The constraint is trademark: the Laurel & Hardy name and recognizable character personas are actively licensed by successor entities, so commercial products that brand themselves on those identities need separate trademark clearance.
Can I use the music from the original soundtrack?

Yes, for the original synchronized score. Marvin Hatley and Leroy Shield composed the music as part of the film, and because the film's copyright lapsed on non-renewal, that original recording is also in the public domain. However, some commercial VHS, DVD, or streaming versions have substituted a newly recorded or digitally remastered audio trackâ€”that replacement recording is independently protected. If the music sounds out of place for a 1932 production, treat the audio as potentially protected and source a copy whose provenance documents it carries the original sound elements.
